title: spark-onramp-ux-and-price-framing-playbook
body:
Executive goal:
Provide a compact, testable playbook for the first 5 minutes a developer spends with Redwood Hosted API: what they see, what they try, and how we frame price so they convert to repeat usage. This doc blends messaging, UX snippets, and pricing-language experiments aimed at increasing time-to-value and reducing cost surprises.

Audience and constraints:
- Primary: backend/frontend engineers and ML engineers who evaluate API ergonomics and unit economics.
- Secondary: platform/infra leads who care about latency predictability and integration guardrails.
- Constraint: marketing page must be truthful about variability (sequence length, batching) while remaining approachable for devs.

Topline value proposition (short):
"Redwood Hosted API: predictable inference costs and developer ergonomics — get to a production-grade prototype in minutes and keep costs from surprising you."

Positioning pillars (unique angles to iterate on):
1) Developer-first flow: one SDK, one token, meaningful defaults. Focus copy on fast local loop and sample apps that run on minimal config.
2) Cost predictability: show an immediate "cost preview" for the request they just typed (estimate per-call and per-1k-tokens).
3) Graceful degradation: automatic fallbacks to cheaper variants when SLAs are flexible — sell reliability instead of raw throughput.
4) Production bridge: clear path from hosted to Dedicated or Private with identical API surface.

Competitive callouts (what to own vs what to concede):
- Many providers emphasize raw model access and more models. We should not compete on model count. Instead own "serving economics + dev ergonomics".
- Some vendors bury latency/cost tradeoffs. Our differentiator: transparent per-route metrics and a cost preview in the quickstart.
- Where others pitch "enterprise-only" SLAs, lead with "free-to-try, then predictable reserved options" to reduce friction.

Quickstart UX & content flow (5-minute path) — required screens and copy snippets:
1) Landing CTA: "Try an example — no credit card needed" (button).
2) Inline playground: prefilled prompt + small "Estimate cost" pill. Tooltip: "Estimated cost: $0.007 (25 tokens) — actual depends on length & batching".
3) SDK sample (node/python) collapsed by default; visible buttons: "Copy snippet" and "Run in Playground".
4) Starter app generator: "Create a demo repo" modal with options: simple chat, summarizer, embedding search. Microcopy: "Ready-to-run: repo + infra-as-code for a 5-minute demo."

Example microcopy options for the pricing line (A/B experiments):
Variant A (transparent, anchors on tokens): "Pay per token. Example: a 200-token response costs ~ $0.016. We show estimated cost before you call."
Variant B (session-first for simplicity): "Pay per session for short experiments. Sessions bundle prompt + response for easier budgeting (trial credit converts to $/session)."
Variant C (hybrid with preview): "Metering by token with a session preview: see a projected cost for this run and a daily budget control."

Suggested A/B tests (priority order):
- Test cost preview UI vs no preview on conversion-to-second-call in first 48 hours. Metric: % of users making a second API call.
- Test token-metered language vs session-bundled language on friction + support tickets about "why was my bill higher than expected?". Metric: billing support rate / new-users.
- Test sample-app generator prominence (modal) vs tucked-in repo link on time-to-first-deploy. Metric: time from signup to "Hello world" repo creation.

Pricing language guardrails (do's and don'ts):
Do:
- Use example math to anchor expectations (show one or two canonical example calls).
- Surface variability: "cost depends on prompt+response length and model variant".
- Offer a "cost simulator" in the playground.
Don't:
- Use opaque terms like "credits" without mapping to dollars/tokens.
- Promise a single number across all workloads.

Short scripts for partner-facing demos (30s, 90s):
30s: "Redwood gives a single API that scales from prototype to production. Try our playground to run a sample request — see an estimated cost before you run and copy the SDK to your app in seconds."
90s: "Developers want speed and predictable economics. Start with our playground: pick a sample app, preview the estimated cost for your input, then copy a one-file SDK snippet. If you need more capacity later, Dedicated gives reserved throughput with the same API and tracing so you don't rewrite integrations."

Landing page hero experiments (copy variants):
- Emphasize speed: "Ship an LLM endpoint in minutes — consistent latency, predictable price."
- Emphasize economics: "Build with an inference API that makes cost visible, not surprising."
- Emphasize developer ergonomics: "One SDK. One request. No surprises."

Examples of quickstart copy blocks (unique tone):
- Onboarding banner: "Want to see cost before you call? Type below and click Estimate — we'll show you the expected charge."
- After first call modal: "Nice! That call cost $0.01. Ready to add a route and pin model version for consistent results?" Button: "Pin model & create route"

Developer checklist for docs & SDKs (must-haves for frictionless conversion):
- Minimal credential setup (single API key with scoped tokens).
- Copy-paste SDK snippet that runs with no configuration.
- One-click 'Create demo repo' that boots a sample app in under 5 minutes.
- Cost preview in playground + downloadable usage CSV.
- Troubleshooting section: interpreting cost variances, batching behavior, and KV cache hints.

Metrics for success (30/60/90 day):
- 30d: % of trial signups that make >= 2 API calls (goal 45%).
- 60d: Time-to-first-demo-repo creation (goal median < 20 minutes).
- 90d: Billing support rate for trial users (goal < 2% of trials).

Rollout plan for copy + experiments:
Week 0: implement cost-preview UI in playground and add the A/B test scaffolding.
Week 1–3: launch Variant A/B testing for pricing copy (token vs session vs hybrid).
Week 4–6: expose starter-app generator to 30% of new signups and measure time-to-repo.
Week 7: iterate on the top-performing copy and roll to 100%.

Open questions and known risks:
- How accurate and conservative should the "estimate" be? Over-promising (low estimate) will frustrate users; conservative estimates may deter experimentation. Need to define the default margin (e.g., +10% buffer).
- Batching behavior can dramatically change realized per-token costs for high-throughput apps. Does the playground simulator need to surface batching assumptions?
- Support load: making cost visible may increase short-term support questions — ensure a short FAQ and in-product help.

Appendix: sample inline SDK snippet (microcopy friendly)
Node (collapsed):
const Redwood = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY });
const res = await client.generate({ model: 'rwd-small', prompt: 'Summarize this text' });
// Estimated cost: $0.005 (previewed in playground)

Closing note: prioritize reducing the cognitive load for the first loop. Developers who understand cost and can run a real sample in under 5 minutes are disproportionately likely to convert to paid and to scale into Dedicated or Private. This playbook should be treated as a living doc — capture test results in JIRA: GT-8210 and iterate quarterly.
